lessons.title: Discovery rules and reading a failure report
lessons.objective: Know exactly which files and functions pytest collects, and read an assertion-introspection failure diff fluently.

blocks.text:
pytest collects by **convention**, not registration. `testpaths = ["tests"]` in `pyproject.toml` says where to look; inside, a file must match `test_*.py` and a function must be named `test_*` to become a test. Everything else is ignored silently.

On a failed `assert`, pytest's **assertion introspection** rewrites the bytecode so the report shows the compared values and a diff — that is why `assert response.payload == {...}` prints both dicts instead of a bare `AssertionError`.

`conftest.py` is scoped to its directory tree: fixtures in `tests/conftest.py` exist only for tests under `tests/`.
blocks.more: Collection order is alphabetical by directory then file, and within a file, top to bottom. `-v` prints one line per collected test as `path::test_name PASSED/FAILED`; the short test summary (`-ra`, already in addopts) recaps non-passing tests at the bottom. Assertion rewriting only applies to test modules and conftest plugins pytest imports itself — helper modules imported normally keep plain asserts, which is one reason helpers should return values and let the test function assert. Renaming `test_status.py` to `status_check.py` or moving it out of `tests/` makes it vanish from the run with no error — the most common 'pytest isn't running my test' cause.

blocks.question: You copy a test file to `checks/test_ready_probe.py` at the repo root and run bare `pytest`. What happens to it?
options: It is collected because the name matches test_*.py
It is collected because pytest scans the whole repo
It is skipped — testpaths limits collection to tests/
pytest errors because the file is outside tests/
blocks.reveal: `testpaths = ["tests"]` restricts default collection to the `tests/` directory, so the file is silently ignored — no error, no warning. It only runs if you pass its path explicitly. Silent skipping is why discovery rules are worth knowing cold.

blocks.instructions:
First, see a clean verbose run:

```pytest -v
```

Note the node IDs (`tests/test_status.py::test_status_request_returns_ready`) and the summary line. Now produce a **deliberate** failure in a scratch copy that lives outside the repo's tracked files (evidence/ is gitignored):

```New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force evidence\exercises
Copy-Item tests\test_status.py evidence\exercises\test_status_broken.py
Copy-Item tests\conftest.py evidence\exercises\conftest.py
```

(bash: `mkdir -p evidence/exercises && cp tests/test_status.py tests/conftest.py evidence/exercises/ && mv evidence/exercises/test_status.py evidence/exercises/test_status_broken.py`)

The conftest copy is required — fixtures are scoped to their directory tree, so `lab_client` does not exist under `evidence/exercises/` without it. Edit `evidence\exercises\test_status_broken.py`: in `test_status_request_returns_ready`, change `"READY"` to `"NOTREADY"`. Then run it and read the diff carefully:

```pytest -v evidence\exercises\test_status_broken.py
```

Find the `assert` line, the `-`/`+` dict diff showing expected NOTREADY vs actual READY, and the `1 failed, 1 passed` summary.

blocks.description: Runs your deliberately broken copy. This check PASSES only when the test FAILS — the failure, and its introspection diff, are the intended artifact. It requires pytest's rewritten-assertion output specifically: `raise RuntimeError("NOTREADY")` also exits nonzero and also prints the word, and produces none of the diff this lesson is about reading.

args.success_note: The broken assertion failed exactly as designed, and the report contains the NOTREADY diff — you produced and read a real failure signature.

blocks.question: In the failure diff, why can pytest show the full contents of both dicts instead of just 'assert False'?
options: The DUT logs both values to dut.log
pytest rewrites assert bytecode in test modules to capture the compared values
LabClient stores every payload in a global registry
The -v flag re-runs the test with tracing enabled
blocks.explanation: Assertion introspection is an import-time bytecode rewrite of test modules. The rewritten assert records the operands, so a failure report can render the actual vs expected values and a diff — no logging or tracing involved.

blocks.question: A teammate says their new test file 'isn't being run' and there is no error. Name the two discovery rules you would check first, and why the failure is silent.
blocks.sample_answer: Check that the file is under the testpaths directory (tests/) and that both the file (test_*.py) and functions (test_*) match the naming conventions. Collection is by convention, so a mismatch means the file is simply never collected — there is nothing to error on.

hints.text: The failure is the goal of the exercise. If pytest exits 0 on the broken copy, you have NOT done it — find out why the diff never happened.
If you see 'fixture lab_client not found' instead of an assertion diff, you skipped the conftest.py copy — fixtures only exist in the directory tree that defines them.

The edit is one word in evidence/exercises/test_status_broken.py: the expected dict in test_status_request_returns_ready should say 'NOTREADY' where the original says 'READY'. The DUT still answers READY; the mismatch is the lesson.

lessons.title: Fixtures: dependency injection and scope
lessons.objective: Explain how pytest injects fixtures by parameter name, and why the DUT is session-scoped while the client is function-scoped.

blocks.text:
A test never calls a fixture. It **declares a parameter**, and pytest matches the parameter name to a registered fixture, builds it, and passes the value in. `def test_x(lab_client: LabClient)` is a dependency injection request.

Fixtures compose: `lab_client` declares `dut` as a parameter, so requesting `lab_client` transitively builds `dut`.

**Scope** controls lifetime: `dut` is `scope="session"` (built once per run), `lab_client` is function-scoped (fresh TCP connection per test). `yield` fixtures run teardown code after the yield — `dut` terminates the process at session end.
blocks.more: Scope choices are cost/isolation trade-offs. Spawning a process per test (function scope) would make the 6-test suite start 6 simulators — slow and port-hungry, with no extra isolation since the DUT is stateless between requests. The client connection, by contrast, is cheap and stateful (the simulator logs client_disconnected, and a stale socket could mask a hang), so per-test is correct. `dut` also performs readiness polling before yielding and hard cleanup after — fixture teardown is where resource guarantees live, which is why the suite can survive a hung test without leaking a simulator process. `test_cleanup.py::test_dut_process_is_running_during_session` asserts mid-session that the process handle is still alive — evidence about the harness itself.

blocks.question: Run `pytest tests/test_cleanup.py tests/test_status.py tests/test_protocol.py` — 8 tests across 3 files, 4 of which request `lab_client` and 4 `dut` directly. How many simulator processes start?
options: 8 — one per test
8 — one per fixture request
3 — one per file
1 — session scope builds dut once
blocks.reveal: (The whole `tests/` tree is much larger now and several of its suites spawn DUTs of their own, so this counts only the three files that share this fixture.) `dut` is declared `@pytest.fixture(scope="session")`: the first request builds it (spawn + readiness poll), every later request reuses the same RunningDut, and teardown kills the process once at session end. lab_client being function-scoped only means a new TCP connection per test — to the same process.

blocks.instructions:
Watch fixture setup/teardown happen by scope. Run:

```pytest -v --setup-show tests/test_cleanup.py tests/test_status.py tests/test_protocol.py
```

(bash identical). In the output, find `SETUP S dut` appearing exactly **once** before the first test, `SETUP F lab_client` appearing before **every** test that requests it, and the matching `TEARDOWN` lines — `TEARDOWN S dut` only after the last test.

Then open `tests/conftest.py` and trace the chain: `lab_client` requests `dut`; `dut` requests `evidence_dir`; `evidence_dir` reads the `EVIDENCE_DIR` env var (this is how CI sandboxes the evidence tree). Finally run the two files that prove process state and protocol behavior agree:

```pytest -v tests\test_cleanup.py tests\test_status.py
```

blocks.description: Runs the process-state test and the status tests together: the session-scoped DUT must be alive mid-session and answer status requests within the same run.

args.success_note: One session-scoped DUT served all three tests: the process was provably alive during the session and answered both status assertions.

blocks.question: Why is making `dut` session-scoped safe here, rather than a test-isolation bug?
options: pytest restarts crashed fixtures automatically
The DUT is stateless across requests, so sharing the process leaks nothing between tests
Session scope runs tests in parallel to save time
lab_client reconnects, which resets the simulator's memory
blocks.explanation: Session scope shares one process across all tests; that is only sound when the resource carries no per-test state. The simulator answers each request independently (verified by test_protocol.py follow-ups), so the savings — one spawn instead of six — cost no isolation.

blocks.question: In your own words: how does a value produced by the `dut` fixture end up inside a test that never mentions `dut` at all?
blocks.sample_answer: pytest resolves fixtures transitively by parameter name: the test asks for lab_client, lab_client declares dut as its own parameter, so pytest builds dut first and injects it into lab_client, which injects the client into the test. The dependency chain is driven entirely by parameter names.

hints.text: Nobody calls these functions. The mechanism is name matching: a parameter named X requests the fixture named X.
Read the decorators in tests/conftest.py: scope='session' on dut, default (function) scope on lab_client — then look at lab_client's parameter list to see the chaining.
Run `pytest --setup-show tests` and count the letters: 'S' setups happen once per session, 'F' setups once per test function. One S for dut, many F for lab_client.

lessons.title: parametrize and markers: one function, many cases
lessons.objective: Write a parametrized pure-unit test of build_response() error paths, with each case traced to REQ-PROTO-001 via a registered marker.

blocks.text:
`@pytest.mark.parametrize` turns one test function into **N independently reported cases**: each parameter set gets its own node ID (`test_x[case-id]`), its own pass/fail, its own JUnit testcase. One failing case does not hide the others.

`@pytest.mark.requirement("REQ-PROTO-001")` attaches metadata. The marker must be **registered** — `pyproject.toml` declares it under `markers = [...]` and addopts carries `--strict-markers`, so a typo'd marker is a hard error, not a silent no-op. `pytest.param(..., marks=..., id=...)` attaches a marker and a readable ID to a single parameter set.

`build_response()` is pure — no socket, no fixture — so these cases need no DUT.
blocks.more: Parametrize arguments map positionally to the function's parameter names: `@pytest.mark.parametrize(("message", "expected_error"), [...])` fills `def test_x(message, expected_error)`. Always give explicit `id=` strings (or pytest derives ugly ones from reprs) — the IDs appear in node IDs, verbose output, and JUnit names, i.e. in your evidence. The requirement marker is what the traceability CSV keys on: `requirements/traceability.csv` links REQ-PROTO-001 to test node IDs, so a marker that does not survive collection breaks the audit chain. `--strict-markers` exists precisely because an unregistered marker name fails silently without it — in a requirements-evidence context, silent is unacceptable.

blocks.question: A function decorated with `@pytest.mark.parametrize` over 3 parameter sets is collected. How many lines does `pytest -v` print for it, and what happens if case 2 fails?
options: 1 line; the whole function is marked failed
3 lines; cases 1 and 3 still run and report independently
3 lines; pytest stops after case 2 fails
1 line; parametrize only affects JUnit output
blocks.reveal: Each parameter set is a separate collected item with its own node ID (test_x[list-input], etc.), so -v prints 3 lines and each case reports independently — a failure in one case neither skips nor masks the others. That independence is exactly why error-path matrices belong in parametrize.

blocks.instructions:
Create `tests/test_build_response.py` — a pure-unit test of the three error branches in `simulator/simulator.py::build_response`, one parametrized function, every case marked REQ-PROTO-001:

- a **list** input (not a dict) → `error_code` `INVALID_MESSAGE_TYPE`
- `{"sequence": 1}` (no command key) → `MISSING_COMMAND`
- `{"command": "selfdestruct", "sequence": 2}` → `UNSUPPORTED_COMMAND`

Use `@pytest.mark.parametrize(("message", "expected_error"), [...])` with three `pytest.param(...)` entries, each carrying `marks=pytest.mark.requirement("REQ-PROTO-001")` and a readable `id=`. Assert `response["status"] == "error"` and `response["error_code"] == expected_error`.

Then run it verbose and confirm three separate node IDs, all passing:

```pytest -v tests\test_build_response.py
```

Also run `pytest --markers` and find the registered `requirement` marker in the list — that registration is what makes `--strict-markers` accept your file.

blocks.description: Parses tests/test_build_response.py and requires one function to be both parametrized and marked REQ-PROTO-001. Checking those separately would accept a parametrized test sitting next to a marked one — two functions, no link — and searching the text would accept either word in a comment.

args.success_note: tests/test_build_response.py parametrizes its cases and carries the REQ-PROTO-001 marker — traceable by construction.

blocks.description: Runs your parametrized test: all three error-path cases must pass against the real build_response().

args.success_note: All three parametrized cases passed and each was recorded as its own JUnit testcase, under the id you gave it — the error matrix is executable evidence for REQ-PROTO-001, not one test with a plural name.

blocks.question: Why pair --strict-markers with a requirements-evidence workflow — what specific failure does it prevent?
blocks.sample_answer: Without --strict-markers, a misspelled or unregistered marker is silently accepted, so a test could lose its requirement link without anyone noticing and the traceability evidence would quietly go stale. Strict markers turn that silent gap into a collection error, because every marker must be registered in pyproject.toml.

hints.text: One function, three rows of data. The marker goes on each row via pytest.param, not on the function — look at how tests/test_protocol.py uses the requirement marker for style.

Signature shape: @pytest.mark.parametrize(('message', 'expected_error'), [pytest.param(<input>, '<ERROR_CODE>', marks=pytest.mark.requirement('REQ-PROTO-001'), id='...'), ...]) over def test_build_response_error_cases(message, expected_error). Import build_response from simulator.simulator.

The three parameter rows: (['status'], 'INVALID_MESSAGE_TYPE', id='list-input'), ({'sequence': 1}, 'MISSING_COMMAND', id='missing-command'), ({'command': 'selfdestruct', 'sequence': 2}, 'UNSUPPORTED_COMMAND', id='unsupported-command'). Body: response = build_response(message); assert response['status'] == 'error'; assert response['error_code'] == expected_error.

Full file:
```"""Pure-unit tests for build_response() error paths — no DUT required."""

from __future__ import annotations

import pytest

from simulator.simulator import build_response


@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    ('message', 'expected_error'),
    [
        pytest.param(['status'], 'INVALID_MESSAGE_TYPE', marks=pytest.mark.requirement('REQ-PROTO-001'), id='list-input'),
        pytest.param({'sequence': 1}, 'MISSING_COMMAND', marks=pytest.mark.requirement('REQ-PROTO-001'), id='missing-command'),
        pytest.param({'command': 'selfdestruct', 'sequence': 2}, 'UNSUPPORTED_COMMAND', marks=pytest.mark.requirement('REQ-PROTO-001'), id='unsupported-command'),
    ],
)
def test_build_response_error_cases(message: object, expected_error: str) -> None:
    response = build_response(message)
    assert response['status'] == 'error'
    assert response['error_code'] == expected_error
```
